question_text:
An 82-year-old woman from a nursing home in Toowoomba, Qld, is brought in after three days of increasing drowsiness. She has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. She is drowsy but rousable. Pulse 112/min, BP 98/60 mmHg, dry mucous membranes.

Investigations:
- Blood glucose 46 mmol/L
- Sodium 149 mmol/L (135–145)
- Calculated serum osmolality 352 mOsm/kg (275–295)
- Capillary ketones (β-hydroxybutyrate) 0.6 mmol/L
- Venous pH 7.34, bicarbonate 21 mmol/L

Which one of the following best explains these findings?
options: Hypernatraemic dehydration without a diabetic emergency
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state

---

The JBDS guideline describes HHS as hypovolaemia with osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg and marked hyperglycaemia (above 30 mmol/L), without significant ketonaemia or acidosis. She meets all of these: osmolality 352, glucose 46, ketones 0.6, pH 7.34, bicarbonate 21. The distinction affects treatment. In HHS, IV fluids come first and insulin is held until glucose stops falling, unless there is significant ketonaemia.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
HHS: osmolality above 320, glucose above 30 mmol/L, hypovolaemia, and no significant ketonaemia or acidosis.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Joint British Diabetes Societies. The Management of Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS) in Adults (Feb 2022)", "url": "https://abcd.care/sites/default/files/site_uploads/JBDS_Guidelines_Current/JBDS_06_The_Management_of_Hyperosmolar_Hyperglycaemic_State_HHS_%20in_Adults_FINAL_0.pdf"}
subtopic: Hyperglycaemic emergency: HHS rather than DKA

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: DKA needs significant ketonaemia (≥3 mmol/L) with acidosis (pH <7.3 or bicarbonate <15). She has neither.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: A mixed picture needs both hyperosmolality and significant ketonaemia or acidosis. Her ketones and pH are near normal.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Her pH and bicarbonate are near normal, so she has no significant acidosis.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: A glucose of 46 mmol/L with osmolality of 352 is a hyperglycaemic emergency, not simple dehydration.

key_takeaways: HHS: osmolality above 320, glucose above 30 mmol/L, hypovolaemia, and no significant ketonaemia or acidosis.
guideline_reference: {"name": "Joint British Diabetes Societies. The Management of Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS) in Adults (Feb 2022)", "url": "https://abcd.care/sites/default/files/site_uploads/JBDS_Guidelines_Current/JBDS_06_The_Management_of_Hyperosmolar_Hyperglycaemic_State_HHS_%20in_Adults_FINAL_0.pdf"}

question_text:
A 46-year-old woman presents to a Brisbane emergency department four hours after taking an unknown number of her mother's gliclazide modified-release tablets. On arrival her blood glucose was 2.1 mmol/L and she was given 50 mL of 50% glucose IV. A 10% glucose infusion was then started. Over the next two hours her glucose falls to 3.2 mmol/L twice despite the infusion. She is alert and her observations are otherwise normal.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next treatment?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Octreotide

---

Sulfonylureas trigger ongoing insulin release, and repeated glucose boluses make it worse by stimulating more secretion. Octreotide suppresses insulin release. Queensland Poisons Information Centre antidote guidance recommends octreotide for sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia (BSL <4.0 mmol/L) after the first glucose correction.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Recurrent hypoglycaemia after a sulfonylurea overdose needs octreotide, which blocks insulin release, rather than more glucose boluses.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Queensland Poisons Information Centre. Antidote stocking recommendations: Octreotide", "url": "https://www.poisonsinfo.health.qld.gov.au/for-health-professionals/antidote-stocking-recommendations/octreotide"}
subtopic: Sulfonylurea overdose: octreotide for recurrent hypoglycaemia

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Repeated boluses stimulate further insulin release from the sulfonylurea-primed pancreas and cause rebound hypoglycaemia.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Glucagon has a brief effect, relies on liver glycogen and also stimulates insulin release. It is not the treatment for sulfonylurea toxicity.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Corticosteroids have no role in treating sulfonylurea-induced hyperinsulinaemia.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Charcoal may be considered early in a cooperative patient, but it does not treat the hypoglycaemia that is already happening.

key_takeaways: Recurrent hypoglycaemia after a sulfonylurea overdose needs octreotide, which blocks insulin release, rather than more glucose boluses.

question_text:
A 38-year-old man sees his GP in Geelong, Vic. He injected drugs 10 years ago. HCV antibody is positive and HCV RNA is detectable. He has never been treated, and the GP plans to prescribe sofosbuvir/velpatasvir. His liver function tests are mildly raised and full blood count is normal. He takes no medicines. He has never had hepatitis B or HIV testing.

Which one of the following tests is most important to request before starting treatment?
options: Hepatitis B serology (HBsAg, anti-HBc and anti-HBs)
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Hepatitis B serology (HBsAg, anti-HBc and anti-HBs)

---

The Australian HCV guidelines' pre-treatment assessment includes testing for HBV coinfection (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs), HIV and HAV serology, FBE, LFTs, eGFR, INR, a fibrosis assessment (such as APRI), and a review of drug interactions. The guidelines have a separate section on treating HCV with HBV coinfection, because coinfection changes how treatment is monitored and managed.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Before HCV DAA treatment, test for HBV (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs) and HIV, assess fibrosis, and check for drug interactions.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian recommendations for the management of hepatitis C virus infection: Pre-treatment assessment", "url": "https://hepcguidelines.org.au/pre-treatment-assessment/"}
subtopic: Chronic hepatitis C: hepatitis B serology before DAA treatment

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Fibrosis is assessed non-invasively (APRI, FIB-4 or elastography). Biopsy is not needed.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: AFP is used for HCC surveillance in cirrhosis, not as a pre-treatment test for everyone.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Genotype is optional (it 'may be considered') when a pan-genotypic regimen is used.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Hepatitis E serology is not part of the pre-treatment assessment.

key_takeaways: Before HCV DAA treatment, test for HBV (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs) and HIV, assess fibrosis, and check for drug interactions.
guideline_reference: {"name": "Australian recommendations for the management of hepatitis C virus infection: Pre-treatment assessment", "url": "https://hepcguidelines.org.au/pre-treatment-assessment/"}

question_text:
A 34-year-old woman in Hobart, Tas, has had drooping of her left eyelid and double vision for six weeks. Both are worse in the evenings and after reading. On examination she has left ptosis that worsens with sustained upgaze for 60 seconds and variable diplopia. Pupils are equal and reactive. Limb power, reflexes and sensation are normal.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation to confirm the likely diagnosis?
options: Lumbar puncture for CSF oligoclonal bands
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Serum acetylcholine receptor antibodies

---

Fatigable ptosis and diplopia with normal pupils suggest myasthenia gravis. Serum acetylcholine receptor antibodies are the first diagnostic test. They are found in most generalised cases and about half of purely ocular cases. Anti-MuSK antibodies, repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fibre EMG come next if AChR antibodies are negative. CT of the chest is then needed to look for a thymoma.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Fatigable ptosis or diplopia with spared pupils points to myasthenia gravis. Test serum AChR antibodies first.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Healthed (Australian GP education). Clinical Conversations: Myasthenia gravis – a practical approach for GPs, part two", "url": "https://www.healthed.com.au/clinical_articles/clinical-conversations-myasthenia-gravis-a-practical-approach-for-gps-part-two/"}
subtopic: Fatigable ptosis and diplopia: AChR antibody

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: MRI is used if there are signs of a brainstem lesion or if pupils are involved. It does not confirm myasthenia.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: CSF findings are normal in myasthenia. This test is for demyelination.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: CK is normal in myasthenia. It is raised in myopathies.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Standard NCS are normal in myasthenia. Repetitive stimulation, not F-waves, is the relevant neurophysiology test.

key_takeaways: Fatigable ptosis or diplopia with spared pupils points to myasthenia gravis. Test serum AChR antibodies first.
guideline_reference: {"name": "Healthed (Australian GP education). Clinical Conversations: Myasthenia gravis – a practical approach for GPs, part two", "url": "https://www.healthed.com.au/clinical_articles/clinical-conversations-myasthenia-gravis-a-practical-approach-for-gps-part-two/"}

question_text:
A 27-year-old woman in Adelaide, SA, has had pain on moving her right eye and blurred central vision for four days. Visual acuity is 6/36 right and 6/6 left. She has a right relative afferent pupillary defect and reduced red colour saturation, and the right optic disc looks normal. Two years ago she had three weeks of numbness from the waist down that resolved without treatment.

Which one of the following findings would most strongly support a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis?
options: A normal optic disc on fundoscopy
Periventricular and juxtacortical T2 lesions on MRI brain, with one lesion enhancing with gadolinium
A visual evoked potential with prolonged latency in the right eye
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Periventricular and juxtacortical T2 lesions on MRI brain, with one lesion enhancing with gadolinium

---

She has typical demyelinating optic neuritis after an earlier episode suggestive of a spinal cord lesion. MS is diagnosed by showing dissemination in space and time (McDonald criteria). Lesions in typical locations (periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial or spinal) show dissemination in space. Having enhancing and non-enhancing lesions at the same time shows dissemination in time.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In optic neuritis, MRI brain lesions in typical MS locations, with both enhancing and non-enhancing lesions, satisfy dissemination in space and time.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Thompson AJ et al. Diagnosis of multiple sclerosis: 2017 revisions of the McDonald criteria. Lancet Neurol 2018;17:162-73 (full-text copy read)", "url": "https://www.moph.gov.lb/userfiles/files/Quality%26Safety/NationalGuidelines/Diagnosis%20of%20multiple%20sclerosis%202017%20revisions%20of%20the%20McDonald%20criteria.pdf"}
• {"name": "Lancet Neurol DOI", "url": "https://doi.org/10.1016/S1474-4422(17)30470-2"}
subtopic: Optic neuritis: MRI predicts MS risk

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Retrobulbar neuritis usually shows a normal disc. This fits optic neuritis but says nothing about MS.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: This confirms demyelination of the affected nerve that is already clinically apparent, but adds no evidence of spread elsewhere.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: AQP4 antibodies indicate neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, which is a different condition from MS.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: ESR is non-specific. A raised value would make you think of giant cell arteritis or another inflammatory cause, not MS.

key_takeaways: In optic neuritis, MRI brain lesions in typical MS locations, with both enhancing and non-enhancing lesions, satisfy dissemination in space and time.

question_text:
A 78-year-old woman in Bendigo, Vic, is seen by her GP because her daughter has noticed she is slower and shuffling. Over the past two months she has developed a symmetrical resting tremor, bradykinesia and rigidity in both arms. She has gastroparesis and started regular metoclopramide 10 mg three times daily three months ago. She has no other new medicines.

Which one of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
options: Dopamine D2 receptor blockade by metoclopramide
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Dopamine D2 receptor blockade by metoclopramide

---

Symmetrical parkinsonism starting soon after a dopamine antagonist is typical of drug-induced parkinsonism. Metoclopramide is a common cause, especially in older women. The treatment is to stop the drug. Recovery may take weeks to months.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Symmetrical parkinsonism after starting metoclopramide is drug-induced (D2 blockade). Stop the drug.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian Prescriber. Drug-induced movement disorders", "url": "https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/drug-induced-movement-disorders.html"}
subtopic: Drug-induced parkinsonism from metoclopramide

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Idiopathic Parkinson disease is usually asymmetrical at onset. A symmetrical onset that follows a dopamine blocker points to the drug.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Essential tremor is a postural or action tremor without bradykinesia or rigidity.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: NPH causes gait apraxia with urinary incontinence and cognitive decline, not a resting tremor with arm rigidity.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: PSP causes early falls and a vertical gaze palsy, and it does not follow a new drug.

key_takeaways: Symmetrical parkinsonism after starting metoclopramide is drug-induced (D2 blockade). Stop the drug.
guideline_reference: {"name": "Australian Prescriber. Drug-induced movement disorders", "url": "https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/drug-induced-movement-disorders.html"}

question_text:
A 69-year-old man with severe COPD (FEV1 32% predicted) is brought by ambulance to a hospital in Launceston, Tas, with three days of increasing breathlessness and purulent sputum. Paramedics started oxygen at 15 L/min by non-rebreather mask. His SpO2 is now 99%, respiratory rate 24/min and he is drowsy.

Venous blood gas: pH 7.29, pCO2 68 mmHg.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate immediate change to his oxygen therapy?
options: Continue 15 L/min because he is hypoxic from the exacerbation
Change to nasal prongs at 6 L/min aiming for SpO2 above 94%
Give IV sodium bicarbonate to correct the acidosis
Titrate oxygen by Venturi mask to a target SpO2 of 88–92%
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Titrate oxygen by Venturi mask to a target SpO2 of 88–92%

---

High-flow oxygen in COPD can worsen hypercapnia (through V/Q mismatch and the Haldane effect). His drowsiness and acidosis point to this. COPD-X recommends controlled oxygen titrated to SpO2 88–92%, with blood gases repeated. He will also need non-invasive ventilation if the acidosis persists.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In a COPD exacerbation, titrate oxygen to SpO2 88–92%. Over-oxygenation worsens hypercapnic acidosis.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Lung Foundation Australia. COPD-X Plan: X – Manage exacerbations", "url": "https://copdx.org.au/copd-x-plan/x-manage-exacerbations/"}
subtopic: COPD exacerbation: target SpO2 88–92%

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: An SpO2 of 99% is well above target, and the high-flow oxygen is contributing to his hypercapnic acidosis.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Stopping oxygen abruptly can cause dangerous rebound hypoxaemia. Titrate to target instead.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: This target is too high for a COPD patient with hypercapnia.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Respiratory acidosis is managed by controlling oxygen and supporting ventilation, not with bicarbonate.

key_takeaways: In a COPD exacerbation, titrate oxygen to SpO2 88–92%. Over-oxygenation worsens hypercapnic acidosis.
guideline_reference: {"name": "Lung Foundation Australia. COPD-X Plan: X – Manage exacerbations", "url": "https://copdx.org.au/copd-x-plan/x-manage-exacerbations/"}

question_text:
A 26-year-old man who has sex with men attends a sexual health clinic in Darlinghurst, NSW. His routine screen showed a positive pharyngeal NAAT for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, with negative urine and anorectal NAATs. No culture swab was taken. He is treated today with ceftriaxone 500 mg IM and azithromycin 2 g orally. He asks what follow-up testing he needs.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate follow-up test?
options: Repeat pharyngeal NAAT 2 days after treatment
No further testing because the regimen is highly effective
Repeat pharyngeal NAAT 2 weeks after treatment as a test of cure
Repeat urine NAAT only at 3 months
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Repeat pharyngeal NAAT 2 weeks after treatment as a test of cure

---

The Australian STI Management Guidelines recommend a test of cure by NAAT at each infected site 2 weeks after treatment is completed. This is especially important for pharyngeal infection, when no culture was collected before treatment, or when resistance is suspected. If the test of cure is positive, seek specialist advice.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
After treating pharyngeal gonorrhoea, do a test of cure by NAAT 2 weeks after treatment.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian STI Management Guidelines. Gonorrhoea", "url": "https://sti.guidelines.org.au/sexually-transmissible-infections/gonorrhoea/"}
subtopic: Pharyngeal gonorrhoea: timing of test of cure

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: NAAT can detect residual non-viable DNA for days after treatment. Testing at 2 days risks a false-positive result.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: A test of cure is still recommended for pharyngeal gonorrhoea.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: There is no useful serological test for gonorrhoea.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Retesting at 3 months is for reinfection. It does not replace a site-specific test of cure.

key_takeaways: After treating pharyngeal gonorrhoea, do a test of cure by NAAT 2 weeks after treatment.
guideline_reference: {"name": "Australian STI Management Guidelines. Gonorrhoea", "url": "https://sti.guidelines.org.au/sexually-transmissible-infections/gonorrhoea/"}

question_text:
A 64-year-old woman on a medical ward in Darwin, NT, is being treated for community-acquired pneumonia with azithromycin. She also takes citalopram and has had diarrhoea for two days. Her monitor shows recurrent runs of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a twisting QRS axis that end on their own. Between episodes she is alert, BP 122/74 mmHg, and her ECG shows sinus rhythm with a QTc of 590 ms.

Serum potassium is 3.1 mmol/L (3.5–5.2).

In addition to stopping QT-prolonging drugs and replacing potassium, which one of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: Magnesium sulfate 5 mmol intravenously over 10 minutes
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Magnesium sulfate 5 mmol intravenously over 10 minutes

---

This is torsades de pointes from an acquired long QT (macrolide, SSRI, hypokalaemia, possibly hypomagnesaemia from diarrhoea). ANZCOR Guideline 11.9 says to treat immediately: stop all QT-prolonging drugs, correct electrolytes (especially potassium), and give IV magnesium 5 mmol over 10 minutes. This can be repeated once and followed by 20 mmol over 4 hours. Pacing or isoprenaline may be needed to prevent relapse. Amiodarone should be avoided because it can make things worse. Synchronised cardioversion is for adverse signs.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Torsades: stop QT-prolonging drugs, correct potassium, give IV magnesium 5 mmol over 10 minutes, and avoid amiodarone.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "ANZCOR Guideline 11.9 – Managing Acute Dysrhythmias", "url": "https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-9-managing-acute-dysrhythmias"}
subtopic: Torsades de pointes: IV magnesium

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: ANZCOR states amiodarone should be avoided in torsades because it can worsen the situation.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Sotalol prolongs QT and is contraindicated.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: ANZCOR reserves cardioversion for adverse signs. She is alert and normotensive between self-terminating runs.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Beta-blockade is not the acute treatment for acquired torsades.

key_takeaways: Torsades: stop QT-prolonging drugs, correct potassium, give IV magnesium 5 mmol over 10 minutes, and avoid amiodarone.
guideline_reference: {"name": "ANZCOR Guideline 11.9 – Managing Acute Dysrhythmias", "url": "https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-9-managing-acute-dysrhythmias"}

question_text:
A 55-year-old man in Ballarat, Vic, has had swelling of his legs for two months. He has no diabetes and takes no regular medicines. BP 136/84 mmHg, pitting oedema to the knees.

Investigations:
- Urine albumin:creatinine ratio 620 mg/mmol
- Serum albumin 22 g/L (35–50)
- Creatinine 88 µmol/L (60–110)
- Total cholesterol 9.1 mmol/L
- Urine microscopy: no red cell casts
- Hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV serology negative; ANA negative; complement normal
- Serum anti-phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) antibodies: strongly positive

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Primary membranous nephropathy

---

Anti-PLA2R antibodies are highly specific for primary membranous nephropathy, the commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in middle-aged and older white adults. KDIGO 2021 says a kidney biopsy is no longer required to confirm membranous nephropathy in patients with nephrotic syndrome and a positive anti-PLA2R test. Secondary causes (malignancy, infection, lupus, drugs) should still be looked for.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Strongly positive anti-PLA2R antibodies in adult nephrotic syndrome point to primary membranous nephropathy.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "KDIGO 2021 Glomerular Diseases Guideline – Executive summary (Kidney Int)", "url": "https://kdigo.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/KDIGO-2021-GD-Guideline-Executive-Summary.pdf"}
subtopic: Nephrotic syndrome in an adult: anti-PLA2R and membranous nephropathy

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Minimal change is the main cause in children and can occur in adults, but it is not associated with PLA2R antibodies.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: FSGS is a common cause in adults, but PLA2R antibodies are negative.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: IgA nephropathy usually causes haematuria, often after an upper respiratory infection, and rarely causes heavy nephrotic syndrome.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: ANA is negative and complement is normal, which argues against lupus.

key_takeaways: Strongly positive anti-PLA2R antibodies in adult nephrotic syndrome point to primary membranous nephropathy.
guideline_reference: {"name": "KDIGO 2021 Glomerular Diseases Guideline – Executive summary (Kidney Int)", "url": "https://kdigo.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/KDIGO-2021-GD-Guideline-Executive-Summary.pdf"}

question_text:
A 34-year-old woman in Cairns, Qld, had a prolactin level included in tests for fatigue. Her periods are regular, she has no galactorrhoea or headaches, and a pregnancy test is negative. She takes no medicines.

Investigations:
- Prolactin 1,150 mIU/L (<500), unchanged on repeat
- TSH normal
- eGFR normal

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Macroprolactin screening of the serum (for example, polyethylene glycol precipitation)
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Macroprolactin screening of the serum (for example, polyethylene glycol precipitation)

---

Australian Prescriber notes that at least 10% of hyperprolactinaemia is due to macroprolactin, a complex that is cleared slowly from the circulation and is largely biologically inactive. That is why most people with macroprolactinaemia have no symptoms. In a woman with confirmed mild hyperprolactinaemia, no symptoms, and pregnancy, drugs, hypothyroidism and kidney disease excluded, macroprolactin screening comes before pituitary imaging.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Mild hyperprolactinaemia without symptoms: check for macroprolactin before pituitary MRI.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian Prescriber. Hyperprolactinaemia (full text via PubMed Central, PMC5768604)", "url": "https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5768604/"}
subtopic: Mildly raised prolactin without symptoms: check for macroprolactin

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Imaging is used for true (monomeric) hyperprolactinaemia. Doing it first risks finding an incidental lesion.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Visual fields are tested when a macroadenoma is suspected. She has no symptoms and her prolactin is only mildly raised.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Treatment is not indicated until true hyperprolactinaemia from a cause that needs treatment is confirmed.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Dynamic pituitary testing is not indicated.

key_takeaways: Mild hyperprolactinaemia without symptoms: check for macroprolactin before pituitary MRI.
guideline_reference: {"name": "Australian Prescriber. Hyperprolactinaemia (full text via PubMed Central, PMC5768604)", "url": "https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5768604/"}

question_text:
A 72-year-old man in Orange, NSW, has had tingling in both feet for four months and feels more tired. He has had type 2 diabetes for 12 years treated with metformin 1 g twice daily. His HbA1c is 6.9%. He eats a mixed diet. There is reduced vibration sense at the toes.

Investigations:
- Haemoglobin 118 g/L (130–180)
- MCV 104 fL (80–100)
- Serum B12 105 pmol/L (>150)
- Folate normal
- TSH normal

Which one of the following is the most likely cause of his macrocytosis?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Metformin-associated vitamin B12 malabsorption

---

Long-term metformin reduces B12 absorption in the ileum. B12 deficiency can cause macrocytic anaemia and a neuropathy that can be mistaken for diabetic neuropathy. B12 should be checked periodically in long-term metformin users, especially those with anaemia or neuropathy. He needs B12 replacement, and metformin can usually continue.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Long-term metformin can cause B12 deficiency, with macrocytosis and neuropathy. Check B12 in these patients.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian Prescriber. Vitamin B12 deficiency: testing and treatment", "url": "https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/vitamin-B12-deficiency-testing-and-treatment.html"}
subtopic: Long-term metformin: vitamin B12 deficiency

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: This is possible, and intrinsic factor antibodies could be checked, but long-term high-dose metformin is the most likely cause here.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: He eats a mixed diet, so dietary deficiency is unlikely.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: TSH is normal.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Neuropathy alone does not explain macrocytic anaemia with a low B12.

key_takeaways: Long-term metformin can cause B12 deficiency, with macrocytosis and neuropathy. Check B12 in these patients.
guideline_reference: {"name": "Australian Prescriber. Vitamin B12 deficiency: testing and treatment", "url": "https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/vitamin-B12-deficiency-testing-and-treatment.html"}

question_text:
A 70-year-old woman presents to her GP in Mackay, Qld, with two days of burning pain over her right forehead followed by a vesicular rash in the distribution of the right ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve. Valaciclovir is started.

Which one of the following examination findings most strongly predicts eye involvement and the need for urgent ophthalmology review?
options: Vesicles on the tip of the nose
Rash extending to the scalp vertex
Pain over the forehead before the rash
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Vesicles on the tip of the nose

---

Hutchinson sign is vesicles on the tip, side or root of the nose. It means the nasociliary branch of V1 is involved, and that branch also supplies the cornea. It strongly predicts ocular herpes zoster (keratitis or uveitis). Any patient with HZO, and especially Hutchinson sign, red eye or reduced vision, needs prompt ophthalmology assessment with a slit lamp.

---

Hutchinson sign (vesicles on the nasal tip) means nasociliary involvement. Expect ocular zoster and refer urgently.

---

question_text:
A 29-year-old man in Adelaide, SA, has had dysuria and a mild urethral discharge for three weeks. Urine NAATs for chlamydia and gonorrhoea are negative. His symptoms continued after 7 days of doxycycline. A first-pass urine NAAT is now positive for Mycoplasma genitalium.

Which one of the following additional laboratory results will most directly determine his antibiotic regimen?
options: Urethral swab culture for M. genitalium
Gram stain of the urethral discharge
Macrolide-resistance mutation testing on the M. genitalium-positive specimen
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Macrolide-resistance mutation testing on the M. genitalium-positive specimen

---

The Australian STI Management Guidelines report that macrolide resistance in M. genitalium is above 60% in Australia and above 80% in men who have sex with men. They recommend resistance-guided therapy. After doxycycline, susceptible infection is treated with azithromycin (1 g, then 500 mg daily for 3 days), and macrolide-resistant infection with moxifloxacin 400 mg daily for 7 days. NAATs that detect macrolide-resistance mutations make this choice possible.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
For M. genitalium, use resistance-guided therapy: doxycycline, then azithromycin if macrolide-susceptible or moxifloxacin if resistant.

---

question_text:
A 76-year-old man in Wagga Wagga, NSW, collapsed while walking up a hill and recovered within a minute. He has had increasing breathlessness on exertion for three months. He has an ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge radiating to the carotids, with a soft second heart sound. ECG shows sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy.

Which one of the following echocardiographic findings best indicates that he needs aortic valve intervention?
options: Peak velocity 2.8 m/s with a mean gradient of 18 mmHg
Aortic valve sclerosis without restricted leaflet opening
Peak aortic jet velocity 4.4 m/s with a mean gradient of 46 mmHg
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Peak aortic jet velocity 4.4 m/s with a mean gradient of 46 mmHg

---

Severe aortic stenosis is defined by a peak velocity of at least 4 m/s, a mean gradient of at least 40 mmHg or a valve area under 1.0 cm². When a patient with severe AS has symptoms (exertional syncope, angina or breathlessness), surgical or transcatheter valve replacement is indicated, because prognosis is poor without it.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Severe AS (≥4 m/s, mean gradient ≥40 mmHg, AVA <1.0 cm²) with symptoms is an indication for valve replacement.

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Sclerosis is not stenosis and does not need intervention.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: This does not explain his symptoms or carry the same indication.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: A preserved ejection fraction does not by itself indicate the need for intervention.

question_text:
A 48-year-old man presents to an emergency department in Bunbury, WA, with 10 hours of severe constant epigastric pain radiating to his back and vomiting. He drinks about 8 standard drinks a day. Pulse 104/min, BP 128/80 mmHg, temperature 37.6°C. He has epigastric tenderness without peritonism.

Which one of the following blood tests is most useful to confirm the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Serum lipase

---

Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed when at least two of three criteria are met: characteristic pain, raised amylase or lipase (at least three times the upper limit of normal), and imaging findings. Australian Prescriber states lipase is now the preferred test. It is more sensitive, particularly in alcohol-related pancreatitis, and stays raised longer, so the diagnostic window is wider.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Lipase (≥3 × ULN) is the preferred blood test for diagnosing acute pancreatitis.

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.C: CRP helps assess severity at about 48 hours but does not make the diagnosis.

incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Triglycerides help find a cause. They do not confirm pancreatitis.

question_text:
A 61-year-old man in Toowong, Qld, has a PSA of 6.8 µg/L on testing he chose after discussion with his GP. A repeat PSA six weeks later is 7.1 µg/L. Digital rectal examination finds a smooth, mildly enlarged prostate. He has no urinary symptoms and a urine dipstick is normal. He is referred to a urologist.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Multiparametric MRI of the prostate

---

The 2026 Australian guidelines for early detection of prostate cancer recommend multiparametric MRI as the next test after a confirmed raised PSA, before any biopsy. Biopsy is recommended for PI-RADS 4–5, or for PI-RADS 3 with a PSA density of 0.15 or more. This approach avoids unnecessary biopsies and finds fewer insignificant cancers.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
After a confirmed raised PSA, the next test is mpMRI. Biopsy depends on the PI-RADS score and PSA density.

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Staging scans are only done after cancer is diagnosed and its risk is defined.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: The PSA is confirmed raised and he needs further assessment now.

question_text:
A 24-year-old man was tackled during a rugby league match in Penrith, NSW, and now has left upper quadrant pain and left shoulder-tip pain. At a major trauma centre, after 1 L of crystalloid, his pulse is 88/min and BP 128/76 mmHg, stable over an hour. He has left upper quadrant tenderness without peritonism. FAST shows a small amount of free fluid in the left upper quadrant.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: CT abdomen with intravenous contrast in arterial and portal venous phases
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. CT abdomen with intravenous contrast in arterial and portal venous phases

---

The Queensland adult blunt splenic injury guideline states that patients with suspected intra-abdominal injury or bleeding should have a CT abdomen with both arterial and portal venous phases. This grades the injury and shows contrast extravasation (blush). Those findings decide between non-operative management, angioembolisation and surgery in a haemodynamically stable patient.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In stable blunt abdominal trauma, CT with arterial and portal venous phases grades splenic injury and detects a contrast blush.

---

question_text:
A 35-year-old motorcyclist arrives at an emergency department in Albury, NSW, after a high-speed crash. He is agitated and in severe respiratory distress. Pulse 138/min, BP 78/40 mmHg, SpO2 82% on high-flow oxygen. The trachea is deviated to the left, his neck veins are distended, and the right chest is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Urgent chest X-ray to confirm the diagnosis
Immediate decompression of the right chest without waiting for imaging
Rapid sequence intubation before any chest procedure
Bedside echocardiography to look for tamponade
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Immediate decompression of the right chest without waiting for imaging

---

This is a clinical diagnosis of tension pneumothorax with obstructive shock. The RCH trauma guideline states that tension pneumothorax with obstructive shock needs urgent pleural decompression by thoracostomy, using anatomical landmarks within the 'triangle of safety', followed by a chest drain. Treatment must not wait for imaging.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis. Decompress immediately; do not wait for imaging.

---

question_text:
A 22-year-old man fell onto his outstretched arm while skateboarding in Fremantle, WA. His right shoulder is squared off, he holds the arm slightly abducted and externally rotated, and there is a palpable fullness in front of the shoulder. Radial pulse is present.

Before reduction, which one of the following is the most important neurological assessment to document?
options: Sensation over the first dorsal web space
Sensation over the lateral aspect of the upper arm (regimental badge area)
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Sensation over the lateral aspect of the upper arm (regimental badge area)

---

Anterior dislocation can stretch the axillary nerve where it winds around the surgical neck of the humerus. Check and document sensation over the regimental badge area (lateral deltoid) before and after reduction. A review of axillary nerve injury in glenohumeral dislocation warns that preserved sensation there does not rule out motor palsy, so deltoid function must be reassessed after reduction.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In anterior shoulder dislocation, document regimental badge sensation (axillary nerve) before and after reduction.

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: This tests the ulnar nerve.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: This tests C5–6 and the musculocutaneous nerve. It is not the key check here.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: This tests the median nerve.

question_text:
A 74-year-old man who smokes presents to a regional emergency department in Dubbo, NSW, with sudden severe back and left flank pain and a brief collapse. Pulse 112/min, BP 86/54 mmHg. He is alert and talking. There is a tender pulsatile mass in the epigastrium. Bedside ultrasound shows an infrarenal aorta of 7.2 cm.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Give fluids to keep systolic BP above 120 mmHg before transfer
Permissive hypotension while he is alert, with immediate referral to vascular surgery for repair
CT angiogram first, with surgical referral only if rupture is confirmed
IV labetalol to lower blood pressure
Admit under general medicine for analgesia and serial ultrasound
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Permissive hypotension while he is alert, with immediate referral to vascular surgery for repair

---

Suspected ruptured AAA in a patient whose cerebration is preserved should be managed with permissive (controlled) hypotension. Avoid aggressive fluids, which dilute clotting factors and can dislodge the clot. Then arrange immediate transfer for endovascular or open repair. The ESVS 2024 guideline recommends permissive hypotension. A CT angiogram is only done if he is stable enough and it will not delay repair.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
For a ruptured AAA: permissive hypotension while he remains alert, and immediate vascular repair.

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.E: This is a surgical emergency.

question_text:
A 23-year-old man presents to a GP in Newcastle, NSW, with three days of right scrotal pain and swelling that began gradually. He has a new female partner and does not use condoms. Temperature 37.8°C. The right epididymis is swollen and tender, the testis lies normally, and the cremasteric reflex is present. There is no urethral discharge.

Which one of the following specimens is most important to collect before starting antibiotics?
options: First-pass urine for chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT, plus a midstream urine
Scrotal ultrasound before any other test
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. First-pass urine for chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT, plus a midstream urine

---

The Australian STI Management Guidelines recommend collecting first-pass urine (for chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT) and a midstream urine for epididymo-orchitis, plus a urethral swab for MC&S if there is a discharge. In men under 35, sexually transmitted organisms are the usual cause. Doppler ultrasound is only needed if the diagnosis is uncertain. If torsion is suspected, refer urgently without waiting for an ultrasound.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In suspected epididymo-orchitis, collect first-pass urine for chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT and an MSU before treatment.

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Ultrasound is for diagnostic uncertainty. His presentation is typical.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Tumour markers are for a testicular mass, not acute inflammation.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: He is not septic.

question_text:
A 56-year-old man in Rockhampton, Qld, has had severe epigastric pain for three hours that came on suddenly and is now generalised. He takes ibuprofen regularly for knee osteoarthritis. He is lying very still. Pulse 110/min, BP 108/70 mmHg, temperature 37.6°C. His abdomen is rigid with generalised guarding and absent bowel sounds. Lipase is 90 U/L (<60).

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Perforated peptic ulcer

---

Sudden severe epigastric pain that becomes generalised peritonitis (a board-like abdomen in a patient lying still) in a regular NSAID user strongly suggests a perforated peptic ulcer. The WSES guideline notes that a negative erect X-ray does not exclude perforation, so when there are clear signs of peritonitis CT should be the first imaging test. Lipase can rise slightly with perforation, while pancreatitis needs a lipase at least three times normal.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Sudden epigastric pain with peritonitis in an NSAID user suggests a perforated peptic ulcer. Mild lipase rises can occur.

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Biliary colic does not cause generalised peritonitis.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: An MI can cause epigastric pain but not a rigid abdomen.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Mesenteric ischaemia causes pain out of proportion to examination findings early on. A rigid abdomen from the start fits perforation better.

question_text:
A 28-year-old woman presents to an emergency department in Bundaberg, Qld, with five days of worsening sore throat, now worse on the left. She can barely open her mouth, has a muffled 'hot potato' voice and is drooling. Temperature 38.6°C. Her airway is patent and SpO2 is 98% on room air. The left soft palate is swollen and the uvula is pushed to the right.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: ENT referral for drainage (needle aspiration or incision) with intravenous antibiotics
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. ENT referral for drainage (needle aspiration or incision) with intravenous antibiotics

---

Trismus, a hot potato voice and a uvula pushed away from the affected side indicate a peritonsillar abscess (quinsy). The PCH WA guideline lists trismus, a unilateral fluctuant swelling extending to the soft palate and uvular deviation as typical. Management is admission under ENT for IV antibiotics with abscess drainage, plus airway assessment and a dose of IV corticosteroid.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Quinsy: drain (aspirate or incise) and give IV penicillin-based antibiotics.

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Her airway is currently safe.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Tonsillectomy in the acute phase is not routine.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Steroids may be used alongside other treatment, but they do not replace drainage.

question_text:
A 69-year-old woman is on the surgical ward in Townsville, Qld, on day 1 after an open right hemicolectomy. Her urine output has been 15 mL/h for four hours (weight 70 kg). Her IV fluids were reduced overnight. Pulse 106/min, BP 104/62 mmHg, capillary refill 4 seconds. Her catheter flushes freely.

Investigations:
- Creatinine 128 µmol/L (pre-op 72)
- Urea 14.2 mmol/L
- Urine sodium 9 mmol/L
- Fractional excretion of sodium 0.5%

Which one of the following is the most likely cause of her oliguria?
options: Prerenal acute kidney injury due to hypovolaemia
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Prerenal acute kidney injury due to hypovolaemia

---

She is tachycardic with slow capillary refill, her fluids were cut back, the catheter is patent, and her urine sodium is low (<20 mmol/L) with an FENa below 1%. KDIGO notes that a high urine osmolality with low urine sodium in oliguria shows intact tubular function. In this setting that points to a volume-responsive (prerenal) cause. Give a fluid bolus and reassess, keeping in mind KDIGO's caution that such indices do not mean the AKI is benign.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Post-operative oliguria with low urine sodium and FENa below 1% is prerenal. Give fluid and reassess.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury (2012)", "url": "https://kdigo.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/KDIGO-2012-AKI-Guideline-English.pdf"}

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: ATN causes a urine sodium above 40 mmol/L and an FENa above 2%.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The catheter flushes freely.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: A ureteric injury would not fit these urine indices or the fluid history.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: She has a working catheter.

key_takeaways: Post-operative oliguria with low urine sodium and FENa below 1% is prerenal. Give fluid and reassess.

question_text:
A 24-year-old woman at 11 weeks' gestation is admitted to a hospital in Shepparton, Vic, after two weeks of persistent vomiting. She has kept almost nothing down for five days and has lost 6% of her body weight. Pulse 108/min. Urine ketones 3+.

Investigations:
- Sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 3.2 mmol/L
- Glucose 3.9 mmol/L

IV fluids, potassium replacement and antiemetics are planned.

Which one of the following should be given before any glucose-containing IV fluid?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Intravenous thiamine

---

After prolonged vomiting and poor intake, thiamine stores are depleted. Glucose can then precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy. The NSW Health 2022 guideline recommends IV thiamine 100 mg daily when oral intake is poor or IV glucose is needed. Glucose-containing fluids should only be used after thiamine has been given and hyponatraemia excluded. Rehydration uses 0.9% sodium chloride with potassium as needed.

---

In hyperemesis with poor intake, give IV thiamine before glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.

question_text:
A 27-year-old woman presents to an emergency department in Mount Gambier, SA, with sudden severe right iliac fossa pain that began four hours ago while she was exercising, with vomiting. Urine β-hCG is negative. She is very tender in the right adnexa. Pelvic ultrasound shows a 7 cm right ovarian cyst, an enlarged right ovary and free fluid.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?

A. Urgent gynaecology review for laparoscopy

Surgery is laparoscopic de-torsion, keeping the ovary where possible, with oophorectomy if it is not viable. Sudden pain with vomiting, a 7 cm cyst and an enlarged ovary make torsion likely, so she should not wait for further tests.

question_text:
A 22-year-old woman sees her GP in Ipswich, Qld, with severe period pain for four years that is not controlled by regular NSAIDs. She also has pain with deep penetration and painful defecation during her periods. She has had vaginal intercourse and agrees to an internal examination, which shows mild posterior fornix tenderness.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: No investigation; reassure that this is primary dysmenorrhoea
Transvaginal pelvic ultrasound performed by an experienced sonographer
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Transvaginal pelvic ultrasound performed by an experienced sonographer

---

RANZCOG's Australian Living Evidence Guideline on endometriosis (endorsed by the RACGP) notes that more cases can now be diagnosed accurately with non-invasive techniques such as transvaginal ultrasound and MRI. Endometriosis no longer always needs surgery for diagnosis, and it can be diagnosed and managed in primary care. A normal scan does not exclude superficial disease. First-line hormonal treatment can still be offered.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Suspected endometriosis can be investigated first with an expert transvaginal ultrasound. Laparoscopy is not required first.

question_text:
A 19-year-old woman phones a clinic in Wollongong, NSW. She takes a combined oral contraceptive pill. She started her new pack three days ago, two days late after the hormone-free week, and has since missed the pills for day 2 and day 3. She had unprotected sex two nights ago. She feels well.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate advice?
options: Take a pill now; no other precautions needed
Stop the pack and start a new one next week
Take a pill now, use condoms for 7 days, and take emergency contraception
Take two pills now and use condoms for 2 days
Do a pregnancy test now and decide afterwards
explanation:

---

More than one pill missed in week 1 with unprotected sex in the past 5 days: take a pill, use condoms for 7 days, and take EC.

question_text:
A 44-year-old woman with three children sees her GP in Albany, WA, with urine leakage when she coughs, laughs or runs. It began after her last birth. She has no urgency or nocturia. Urinalysis is normal and her BMI is 31 kg/m². Pelvic examination shows no significant prolapse.

question_text:
A 33-year-old woman sees a GP in Canberra, ACT, after her third consecutive first-trimester miscarriage. Each was at 7–9 weeks. She has no other medical history. Her partner is well. Pelvic ultrasound is normal.

Which one of the following investigations is most likely to identify a treatable cause?
options: Inherited thrombophilia screen (factor V Leiden, protein C and S)
Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies, repeated after 12 weeks if positive
Serum progesterone in a non-pregnant cycle
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies, repeated after 12 weeks if positive

---

Antiphospholipid syndrome is the most common acquired thrombophilia and an important treatable cause of recurrent pregnancy loss. The 2024 Australasian RPL guideline lists APS testing as anticardiolipin antibody, lupus anticoagulant and β2-glycoprotein I antibody, using the updated Sydney criteria, which need persistence at least 12 weeks apart. It notes that trials have not shown an association between inherited thrombophilia and RPL, or benefit from LMWH, so inherited thrombophilia screening is not useful.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Recurrent miscarriage: test for antiphospholipid syndrome, confirm at 12 weeks, and treat with aspirin plus heparin in the next pregnancy.

---

question_text:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to a GP in Warrnambool, Vic, at 9 pm with a barking cough and hoarse voice that started that evening, after two days of a runny nose. He has soft stridor only when he is upset. There is no stridor at rest, no chest wall recession, and he is alert and playing. SpO2 98%.

options: A single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg and discharge with safety-net advice
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A 4-year-old boy in Hobart, Tas, has had puffy eyes for one week and now has swollen legs. BP is normal. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein with no blood. question_text:
A 4-week-old breastfed boy is brought to a GP in Kalgoorlie, WA, because he is still jaundiced. He is feeding well and gaining weight. His mother thinks his stools have been pale for a week. His urine is dark yellow.

Investigations:
- Total bilirubin 160 µmol/L
- Conjugated bilirubin 70 µmol/L
- Liver ultrasound: normal liver; gallbladder seen

options: Urgent same-day discussion and referral to paediatric gastroenterology
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Urgent same-day discussion and referral to paediatric gastroenterology

---

A conjugated bilirubin above 20 µmol/L (or more than 20% of the total) is abnormal, and with pale stools it suggests biliary atresia until proven otherwise. RCH guidelines state that a normal ultrasound does not exclude biliary atresia. Urgent referral matters because outcomes of Kasai surgery are better when it is done early.

Prolonged jaundice with conjugated bilirubin above 20 µmol/L or pale stools needs urgent gastroenterology referral. A normal US does not exclude biliary atresia.

question_text:
A 5-year-old girl is brought to an emergency department in Geraldton, WA, with one day of refusing to walk on her right leg. Temperature 38.9°C. She holds her hip flexed and externally rotated and resists all movement.

question_text:
A 26-year-old man with schizophrenia is reviewed by a community mental health team in Footscray, Vic. He still has persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations that stop him working. He had 6 weeks of risperidone, with adherence confirmed because it was given as a long-acting injection at a therapeutic dose, and then 8 weeks of olanzapine 20 mg daily, with adherence confirmed by plasma levels. Neither helped. He does not use substances, and organic causes have been excluded.

Which one of the following best describes his illness, and what does it imply?
options: Schizoaffective disorder needing a mood stabiliser
Treatment-resistant schizophrenia; a clozapine trial should be started promptly
Inadequate trial; continue olanzapine for another 6 months
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Treatment-resistant schizophrenia; a clozapine trial should be started promptly

---

He has had two adequate antipsychotic trials, with confirmed adherence and adequate dose and duration, and still has significant symptoms. This meets the definition of treatment-resistant schizophrenia. The RANZCP-endorsed INTEGRATE guidelines say that if two adequate trials fail, a clozapine trial should be started promptly, aiming for plasma levels of 350–500 ng/mL.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Two adequate antipsychotic trials that have failed define treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Start clozapine promptly.

question_text:
A 32-year-old woman presents to a hospital in Logan, Qld, with sudden weakness of her right leg that began after a stressful week at work. She can barely lift her right leg off the bed. When she is asked to flex her left hip against resistance, strong involuntary extension of the right hip is felt. Reflexes are symmetrical, plantar responses are flexor and sensation is normal. MRI of the brain and spine is normal.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Positive Hoover sign consistent with functional neurological disorder
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Positive Hoover sign consistent with functional neurological disorder

---

A positive Hoover sign means hip extension is weak when tested directly but returns to normal during contralateral hip flexion. It is a positive clinical sign of functional weakness. FND is diagnosed on positive features, not by exclusion alone. It is not feigning. Treatment involves explaining the diagnosis clearly, then physiotherapy and psychological therapy.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Hoover sign is a positive sign of functional weakness. FND is diagnosed on positive features, and it is not feigning.

question_text:
A 20-year-old university student in Newcastle, NSW, tells her GP she binge-eats several times a week and then makes herself vomit. Her BMI is 22 kg/m². She has bilateral parotid swelling and calluses on the backs of her fingers. She feels lightheaded at times.

Which one of the following investigations is most important at this visit?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Serum electrolytes including potassium

---

Self-induced vomiting causes hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis, which can lead to arrhythmias. Australian Prescriber states that a physical examination, FBC, urea and electrolytes (including phosphate) and an ECG are mandatory to assess the physical complications of purging. Hypokalaemia may even be the first clue to an eating disorder. Psychological treatment is eating-disorder-focused CBT.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In bulimia with purging, check potassium (hypokalaemic alkalosis can cause arrhythmia).

question_text:
An 84-year-old woman with Alzheimer disease in a residential aged care facility in Launceston, Tas, has become agitated in the late afternoons over the past five days, calling out and pacing. She communicates little verbally. Staff ask the GP for 'something to settle her'. Her regular medicines have not changed.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate first step in assessment?
options: Assess for delirium, pain and other unmet physical needs such as constipation or urinary retention
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Assess for delirium, pain and other unmet physical needs such as constipation or urinary retention

---

The NSW Health BPSD handbook asks first whether delirium is present and whether the person could be in pain, need the toilet, or have other unmet basic needs. Delirium causes and pain must be treated before behaviour is attributed to dementia. A structured pain tool (for example, the Abbey Pain Scale), examination, bowel and bladder review and a look for infection are first steps. Non-pharmacological strategies come before medication.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
New BPSD: look for delirium, pain and unmet needs first.

question_text:
A 58-year-old man in Toowoomba, Qld, has taken oxazepam 30 mg three times daily for six years. It was first prescribed after a bereavement. He would now like to stop. He has no history of seizures and does not drink alcohol.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate plan?
options: Switch to an equivalent dose of diazepam and reduce gradually over weeks to months
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Switch to an equivalent dose of diazepam and reduce gradually over weeks to months

---

Stopping benzodiazepines abruptly after long-term use risks withdrawal seizures. Australian Prescriber advises a gradual dose reduction over weeks to months, often after switching to diazepam because its long half-life gives a smoother taper.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Stop long-term benzodiazepines with a slow taper, often after switching to diazepam.

question_text:
A new point-of-care test for deep vein thrombosis has a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 70% compared with compression ultrasound.

Which one of the following is the positive likelihood ratio of this test?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. 3.0

---

LR+ = sensitivity ÷ (1 − specificity) = 0.90 ÷ 0.30 = 3.0. A positive result triples the pre-test odds.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
LR+ = sensitivity ÷ (1 − specificity).

---

question_text:
A case–control study in Victoria compares mothers of infants born with a congenital heart defect with mothers of healthy infants. All are asked months after the birth about over-the-counter medicines they took in early pregnancy. Case mothers report more medicine use.

Which one of the following biases is most likely to explain part of this association?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Recall bias

---

Mothers of affected infants are more likely to search their memories and report exposures. This differential misclassification of exposure is recall bias, and it is typical of case–control studies that rely on self-report.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Self-reported past exposures in case–control studies are prone to recall bias.

---

question_text:
In a cohort of 2,000 Queensland farm workers followed for 5 years, 1,000 worked regularly with livestock and 1,000 did not. Leptospirosis was diagnosed in 20 livestock workers and 5 non-livestock workers.

Which one of the following is the relative risk of leptospirosis for livestock work?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. 4.0

---

RR = (20/1000) ÷ (5/1000) = 0.02 ÷ 0.005 = 4.0.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
RR = risk in the exposed ÷ risk in the unexposed.

question_text:
A 24-year-old unvaccinated man returned to Sydney from Southeast Asia nine days ago. He sees a GP with three days of fever, cough, conjunctivitis and coryza, and since this morning a maculopapular rash spreading from his face. The GP isolates him in a separate room. Serology and PCR swabs are collected.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next action regarding public health?
options: Wait for PCR confirmation before notifying
Notify the local public health unit promptly by telephone, without waiting for laboratory confirmation
Notify only if the patient consents
Contact his workplace directly to warn colleagues
No notification needed because he is an adult
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Notify the local public health unit promptly by telephone, without waiting for laboratory confirmation

---

The NSW Health measles control guideline asks emergency departments and medical practitioners to report suspected cases to the local public health unit promptly, and to seek laboratory confirmation in all suspected cases. Early notification of a suspected case allows contact tracing and post-exposure prophylaxis within the time when it works. Cases should stay home until 4 days after rash onset.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Suspected measles: isolate, test and notify the public health unit promptly on clinical suspicion.

---

question_text:
A 46-year-old woman sees her GP in Darwin, NT, with a new 2 cm firm lump in her left breast that she noticed three weeks ago. She asks whether she should book a free BreastScreen mammogram.

question_text:
A 23-year-old woman starting work at an abattoir in Wagga Wagga, NSW, attends for Q fever vaccination. Pre-vaccination testing shows a negative Q fever antibody serology, and the skin test, read 7 days later, is positive (induration 6 mm).

Which one of the following is the most appropriate interpretation and action?
options: She is sensitised and should not be vaccinated
Repeat the skin test in 1 week
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. She is sensitised and should not be vaccinated

---

The Australian Immunisation Handbook states that a positive result on either serology or skin test means the person is sensitised and must not be vaccinated, because of the risk of severe local reactions. Vaccination goes ahead only if both tests are negative.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
